title: Indra and the dream
hookLine: Indra's second try: the dreaming self, lit from within, still weeps
carry: the dreamer isn't the deepest self
last: THE SELF IS NOT THE BODY.

cards: Indra walked back to Prajapati, firewood in hand again, and said: the body can go blind, and die. That can't be the self. True, said Prajapati.
Stay another thirty-two years. When the years were done, he gave a new answer. The one who moves about happily in dreams: that is the self.
It made sense. A dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind, or lame when the body is lame. Indra set off home, pleased.
And again, on the road, he stopped.

teach.b: Because in a dream, Indra saw, the dreamer still suffers. It's as if it's being struck, as if it's being chased. It feels pain.
It even weeps. That's no self beyond sorrow. He turned around a second time.

The Mandukya gives this dreamer a beautiful name: taijasa, the shining one, from tejas, brilliance. Its fourth verse says the dream self knows inward and enjoys the subtle: images, memories, feelings, made of mind.
Commentators explain the name. In a dream there's no sun and no lamp, and yet everything is seen. The dream is lit from within.

In om, it's the second sound, u, between a and m, the way dreaming sits between waking and deep sleep. So the story and the verse agree. Dreaming is a real quarter of the self, a whole world made by the mind.
And it still isn't the deepest self, because what's in it can frighten and grieve. That's the teaching. You are not only the one who acts by day, and not only the one who dreams by night.
Many Hindu teachers name a witness of both, the sakshi, the one who sees, and the path is learning to stand there. Today, nobody has to be asleep to dream. A fight replayed at three in the morning.
A worst case that hasn't happened. A feed that pulls you in. A world lit from within, and it feels completely real.
Indra's question still works: is this the deepest me, or something I'm watching?

how: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya and Gaudapada's Karika are studied together; the comparison between dreaming and waking is a classic subject of that study.

o: a prayer said aloud just before falling asleep
a book of omens for reading what dreams foretell
an Upanishad that calls the dreamer the shining one

s: Indra accepted the dreamer as the deepest self
he saw the dreamer is still chased, feels pain and weeps, and turned back again.
it knows inward; the waking self knows outward.
taijasa comes from a word meaning brilliance
tejas: the dream is lit from within.

games.q: Prajapati says the dreamer is the self. it can't go blind or lame. what's still wrong with it?
o: in dreams it still gets chased, feels pain and weeps.
games.why: Indra wanted a self beyond sorrow. the dreamer, lit from within, still grieves, so he turned back.

practice: Close your eyes and let an image come, a place you love, a face, a color, and notice there's no outer light, yet you can see it: that's the shining one, lighting a world from inside.
Let it fade and another come, and watch them the way you'd watch a dream, without getting pulled in. Then let them all go, and notice what was watching.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad. The second quarter is taijasa, the shining one: the dream state, knowing inward, lit from within.

orig.note: Sanskrit: svapna, dream, sleep; Mandukya 4: the dream state is the field of taijasa.

carryVoice: Your line: the dreamer isn't the deepest self. Even the shining one can weep. Two hundred fifty-five days now.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.9.2–8.10.2 (the dream self; Indra sees it still suffers and weeps)
